records.sourceFile: Why Exercise may be Beneficial in    Concussion Rehabilitation- A Cellular Perspective.pdf

paper.citation: Dech RT, Bishop SA, Neary JP. Why Exercise may be Beneficial in Concussion Rehabilitation: A Cellular Perspective. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2019.
paper.abstract: Concussion diagnosis and rehabilitation have become a prevalent area of research, and exercise is now introduced earlier in recovery. This review aims to refresh the knowledge of concussion from a neurometabolic and broader physiological perspective, using gene expression to show why and how physical activity may optimise recovery at the cellular level.
paper.tldr: Mild, sub-symptom exercise introduced early after concussion may support recovery through cellular signalling, but these links are largely theoretical and too much intensity may be harmful. Use the paper to inform clinical thinking, not as a tested exercise protocol.
paper.methods: Narrative review of concussion pathophysiology and the cellular signalling pathways linked to exercise, with some human and animal studies cited. The text does not describe a systematic search.
paper.findings: The review describes concussion-induced ion dysregulation, energy crisis and impaired neurovascular coupling, and argues that exercise-related pathways (BDNF, CREB, mTOR, PGC-1a) are active in both exercise and concussion. In a cited mouse study, BDNF did not change with exercise in the first 72 hours but increased at 14 to 20 days. Cited human work includes a trial in which home exercise at 80% of the treadmill symptom-threshold intensity shortened recovery compared with stretching, and studies in which absolute rest was not better than usual care with progressive activity.
paper.limitations: This is a narrative review with no described search, and the authors call their rationale technically theoretical. Most human autonomic data are proxy measures, and the cellular evidence for exercise timing comes from mouse studies. The text is an accepted manuscript version, so pagination and volume are not printed.
paper.practicalImplications: Early, mild, sub-symptom activity is favoured over absolute rest in the review's framing, while the acute phase is still described as a time for rest. The review cites estimates of 10 to 15 minutes at 40 to 50% of maximal heart rate for untrained and 15 to 20 minutes at 60 to 70% for trained individuals, and suggests moderate or higher intensity and sessions over 45 minutes may hinder recovery, but these come from other sources and need clinical supervision.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Not applicable. The paper concerns post-concussion exercise, not training prescription for healthy athletes.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review supports introducing mild, sub-symptom exercise early in concussion recovery, not full training. Its cited heart-rate and duration estimates are not return-to-play criteria, and it provides no new outcome or safety data to set clearance thresholds.

paper.citation: Wang Y, Lei SM, Fan J. Effects of Mindfulness-Based Interventions on Promoting Athletic Performance and Related Factors among Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trial. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2023;20:2038.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of 32 randomised trials of mindfulness-based interventions in athletes, with meta-analysis of mindfulness, mindfulness-related psychological components and mental health outcomes. Performance was summarised narratively.
paper.tldr: Across 32 randomised trials in many sports, mindfulness-based training was linked to moderate gains in mindfulness and large gains in related psychological factors such as flow, acceptance and self-compassion, with performance gains reported narratively and no pooled effect on mental health. The evidence base is small and varied, so treat it as a promising option rather than a proven one.
paper.methods: PRISMA-based search of five databases with no date limit, registered on PROSPERO (CRD42022299940). Two reviewers screened and extracted data independently. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool, pooled SMDs were calculated with random-effects models in RevMan 5.4, and publication bias was checked with funnel plots and Egger tests.
paper.findings: Narrative synthesis: the authors report that all included studies showed significant performance improvement. Meta-analysis: mindfulness SMD 0.50 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.83; 3 studies; I2 45%); mindfulness-related psychological components SMD 0.81 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.10; 5 studies; I2 77%); mental health SMD -0.03 (95% CI -0.35 to 0.29; 4 studies; I2 89%). Funnel plots and Egger tests showed no significant publication bias (all P > 0.1). A sensitivity analysis excluding high risk-of-bias studies was consistent with the main results.
paper.limitations: Pooled analyses include only 3 to 5 trials each, with high heterogeneity, and no subgroup analysis was possible. Only English-language studies were searched. The study counts differ across the abstract (seven meta-analysed), results and discussion (nineteen quantitatively analysed), and reference 57 (cited for the ice-hockey RCT) is a coronary-artery-disease paper, so the exact trial set and citations need checking.
paper.practicalImplications: Mindfulness-based training is a reasonable option to consider for athletes who need help with flow, acceptance or self-compassion, with the programme matched to that target. Do not expect a benefit for mental health symptoms, since the pooled result was null. Test any programme against your own squad's outcome measures before relying on it.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The strongest pooled effects are on mindfulness and performance-related psychological factors such as flow and acceptance, so mindfulness is most defensible as a mental-skills tool for competition preparation. The performance benefit itself rests on narrative synthesis of varied measures.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review does not assess rehabilitation or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.
